## Compactness

Compactness is the right generalisation of "closed and bounded" to settings
beyond $\mathbb{R}^n$. Informally, a compact set cannot escape to infinity or
have missing boundary points: any infinite collection of points in it must
*pile up* somewhere inside it. It is the property that lets us extract limits,
and it underlies the extreme value theorem, the fact that $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$
is a compact metric space (see [[metric-spaces]]), and tightness and Prokhorov's
theorem in probability (see [[tightness]]).

## Definitions

:::{.definition data-title="Sequential Compactness"}

A subset $K$ of a [[metric-spaces|metric space]] $X$ is **(sequentially)
compact** if every sequence in $K$ has a subsequence that converges to a point
of $K$.

:::

:::{.definition data-title="Open Cover Compactness"}

An **open cover** of $K\subseteq X$ is a family $\{U_\alpha\}$ of open sets with
$K\subseteq\bigcup_\alpha U_\alpha$. The set $K$ is **compact** if every open
cover has a **finite subcover**, that is, finitely many $U_{\alpha_1},\dots,U_{\alpha_n}$
with $K\subseteq\bigcup_iU_{\alpha_i}$.

:::

In a metric space the two definitions agree (proved below). The open cover
definition is the one used in general [[topology]], where there are no
sequences to speak of.

:::{.example data-title="Examples and Non-Examples"}

- $[0,1]$ and every closed bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is compact, as is any
  finite set.
- $(0,1)$ is not compact: the sequence $1/n$ has no limit in $(0,1)$, and the
  open cover $\{(1/n,1)\}_{n\geq2}$ has no finite subcover.
- $\mathbb{R}$ is not compact: the sequence $n$ has no convergent subsequence, and
  $\{(-n,n)\}$ has no finite subcover.
- In infinite dimensions closed and bounded is not enough. The closed unit ball in
  $(C([0,1]),d_\infty)$ is not compact: $f_n(x)=x^n$ has no uniformly convergent
  subsequence, as its pointwise limit is discontinuous at $1$.

:::

## Basic Properties

:::{.theorem data-title="Compact Implies Closed and Bounded"}

A compact subset $K$ of a metric space is closed and bounded.

:::

:::{.proof}
*Bounded:* if not, fix $x_0\in K$ and choose $x_n\in K$ with $d(x_n,x_0)>n$. Any
subsequence is unbounded, so none converges, contradicting compactness.
*Closed:* let $x_n\in K$ with $x_n\to x$. By compactness a subsequence converges
to some $y\in K$, but also converges to $x$, so $x=y\in K$ by uniqueness of limits.
By the sequential criterion for closed sets in [[metric-spaces]], $K$ is closed.
:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Closed Subsets of Compact Sets"}

A closed subset $F$ of a compact set $K$ is compact.

:::

:::{.proof}
A sequence in $F$ lies in $K$, so has a subsequence converging in $K$; its limit
lies in $F$ since $F$ is closed.
:::

## Heine-Borel

:::{.theorem data-title="Bolzano-Weierstrass"}

Every bounded sequence in $\mathbb{R}^n$ has a convergent subsequence.

:::

:::{.proof}
For $n=1$: every real sequence has a monotone subsequence (call $m$ a *peak* if
$x_m\geq x_k$ for all $k>m$; infinitely many peaks give a decreasing subsequence,
and otherwise after the last peak we can repeatedly find larger terms, giving an
increasing one). A bounded monotone sequence converges, see
[[sequence-convergence]]. For $\mathbb{R}^n$ pass to a subsequence converging in
the first coordinate, then a further one converging in the second, and so on;
after $n$ steps all coordinates converge.
:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Heine-Borel"}

A subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.

:::

:::{.proof}
($\Rightarrow$) is the theorem above. ($\Leftarrow$) A sequence in a bounded set
is bounded, so has a convergent subsequence by Bolzano-Weierstrass, and the limit
lies in the set since it is closed.
:::

## Equivalence of the Definitions

:::{.theorem data-title="Open Cover and Sequential Compactness Agree"}

For a subset $K$ of a metric space, $K$ is open cover compact if and only if it
is sequentially compact.

:::

:::{.proof}
($\Rightarrow$) Let $\{x_n\}\subseteq K$ have no subsequence converging in $K$.
Then every $y\in K$ has a ball $B_y$ containing $x_n$ for only finitely many $n$
(otherwise we could choose $n_1<n_2<\cdots$ with $x_{n_k}\to y$). The balls $B_y$
cover $K$, so finitely many of them do, and then only finitely many indices $n$
exist, a contradiction.

($\Leftarrow$) *Sketch.* Sequential compactness gives (i) **total boundedness**:
for every $\epsilon>0$ finitely many $\epsilon$-balls cover $K$ (otherwise
choose points at distance at least $\epsilon$ from each other, a sequence with
no convergent subsequence), and (ii) a **Lebesgue number** $\delta>0$ for any
open cover, such that every ball of radius $\delta$ lies in a single set of the
cover. Covering $K$ by finitely many $\delta$-balls then yields a finite
subcover.
:::

A metric space is thus compact if and only if it is **complete and totally
bounded**.

## Continuous Functions on Compact Sets

:::{.theorem data-title="Continuous Image of a Compact Set"}

If $f:K\to Y$ is continuous and $K$ is compact, then $f(K)$ is compact.

:::

:::{.proof}
Let $y_n=f(x_n)$ be a sequence in $f(K)$. By compactness a subsequence
$x_{n_k}\to x\in K$, and by continuity $y_{n_k}=f(x_{n_k})\to f(x)\in f(K)$.
:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Extreme Value Theorem"}

A continuous function $f:K\to\mathbb{R}$ on a nonempty compact set attains its
maximum and minimum.

:::

:::{.proof}
$f(K)$ is compact in $\mathbb{R}$, hence closed and bounded by Heine-Borel, so
$\sup f(K)$ and $\inf f(K)$ are finite and belong to $f(K)$.
:::

A continuous function on a compact metric space is also **uniformly continuous**
(Heine-Cantor). Continuous images of compact sets explain why a homeomorphism
$\varphi:\overline{\mathbb{R}}\to[-1,1]$ shows $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ is compact.
